candidate.title: Richard Swinburne vs Bart Ehrman — God and Suffering (2009)
candidate.label: God and Suffering
candidate.sourceNote: Source: the Unbelievable radio debate broadcast on 10 January 2009, moderated by Justin Brierley, preserved in the supplied Bart D. Ehrman channel recording. By explicit editorial approval, this assessment scores only Richard Swinburne and Bart Ehrman in their main exchange and both final summaries, approximately 25:05–1:18:44, excluding programme breaks. This radio debate has no timed formal rounds. Justin Brierley’s arguments and questions remain unscored context; only the two speakers’ own contributions and replies are assessed, and no host argument is credited to either side. Unequal prompting and opportunities to reply are considered. Introductions, listener material, the unrelated prerecorded segment, preliminary biographical interviews and the outro are excluded, with no credit, penalty, inferred concession or failure-to-reply inference from them. Swinburne answers the heaven objection in his final summary, after Ehrman’s last opportunity to respond. Public automatic captions were supplemented by five targeted automated audio checks, not direct human listening.
candidate.scoringNote: Scores are AI-generated estimates of argumentative performance, rather than judgments about worldview truth; the separate AI Contribution does not affect these scores.

con.name: Christian explanations of suffering are inadequate
con.speaker: Bart Ehrman

candidate.summary: Ehrman’s victim-centered, natural-evil, and scriptural challenges outweighed Swinburne’s coherent but incompletely warranted account of responsible freedom, sanctity, redemption, and heaven.

pro.text: the point about heaven is it comes after earth
pro.context: Swinburne’s closing answer distinguishes formative earthly freedom from the settled good character he says can exist later in heaven.

con.text: we should do more because the world is in a very sad shape
con.context: Ehrman closes by separating unsolved explanatory questions from the practical obligation to reduce homelessness, disease, poverty, and starvation.

pro.words: Swinburne limits omnipotence to logically possible acts, contrasts logical with physical constraints, and argues that certain valuable states require allowing suffering.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Swinburne precisely narrows omnipotence to logically possible action, uses the surgeon comparison to distinguish logical from physical limitation, and thereby answers Ehrman’s initial appearance of outright contradiction. Principal limitation: The compatibility result depends on the further, only introduced proposition that relevant goods cannot exist without permitted suffering, so it does not yet establish that actual suffering is necessary, proportionate, or explanatorily adequate. Live burden: His side must identify those goods, defend their logical dependence on suffering, and connect possibility-level reconciliation to the victim-centered moral conditions developed later. Locked score: 83/100 reflects unusually clear modal reasoning and direct engagement, moderated by an evidentiary bridge that remains asserted rather than demonstrated at this stage.

con.words: Ehrman frames the tension among divine power, divine love, and suffering, requiring either a rejected premise or an adequate extenuating circumstance.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman states the three propositions cleanly, distinguishes denying one from supplying an extenuating circumstance, and makes explanatory adequacy rather than mere doctrinal repetition the debate’s central burden. Principal limitation: The opening establishes a prima facie tension rather than a contradiction under every defensible account of omnipotence or love, and it does not yet compare particular Christian explanations. Live burden: His side must show that Swinburne’s proposed circumstances fail on their own stated conditions without treating the initial triad as a completed deductive disproof. Locked score: 85/100 rewards the motion-level framing, conceptual clarity, and calibrated appearance language, while reserving judgment on whether the subsequent victim, natural-evil, and scriptural challenges defeat the offered reconciliation across the full range of suffering presented in the exchange.

pro.words: Swinburne values consequential responsibility and argues that creator authority permits harm only when victims receive an overall beneficial life or compensating benefits.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Swinburne moves beyond bare choice to consequential responsibility, explains why others’ welfare must genuinely depend on agents, and explicitly conditions divine permission on benefit to those who suffer. Principal limitation: The parental-treatment analogy does not independently establish that creating a person confers enlarged authority over nonconsenting victims, while the promised overall benefit remains unverified for the cases under dispute. Live burden: He must demonstrate that actual victims receive sufficient subject-centered benefit and that responsibility could not be preserved through less destructive conditions, rather than relying on creator status alone. Locked score: 78/100 recognizes a substantive and carefully qualified moral framework, but discounts the underdefended transfer from nurturing parental authority to divine permission of severe suffering.

con.words: Ehrman targets Swinburne’s own benefit condition with famine victims, while conceding human-caused suffering and separating natural disasters from free choices.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman accepts free will’s genuine explanatory reach, then tests Swinburne’s explicit permission condition against victims whose lives appear nonbeneficial and against suffering not produced by human agency. Principal limitation: His famine quantities and conclusion about whole-life benefit remain reported debate claims rather than independently established evidence, so the examples pressure the condition without conclusively measuring every victim’s welfare. Live burden: He must sustain the victim-centered challenge while allowing that human choices explain some suffering and that Swinburne may offer additional goods beyond the initial freedom defense. Locked score: 86/100 reflects excellent responsiveness, charitable concession, and direct burden contact, with a modest reservation for the unverified empirical scale and compressed whole-life assessment.

pro.words: Swinburne argues natural suffering creates otherwise unavailable choices for sufferers and observers, whose repeated responses form character and advance possible holiness.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Swinburne supplies an intelligible mechanism from natural suffering through serious response choices to character formation, extending his agency account beyond harms directly caused by human wrongdoing. Principal limitation: Showing that suffering creates opportunities does not establish that suffering at the observed severity is needed, proportionate, or beneficial to each victim under his earlier authorization condition. Live burden: He must connect character-forming opportunity to the justification of particular sufferers’ costs, explain why less destructive circumstances would not suffice, and avoid treating observers’ development as automatically compensating victims. Locked score: 76/100 credits a relevant, coherent natural-evil proposal and clear causal sequence, while substantially discounting its asserted counterfactual necessity and unresolved victim-level moral adequacy.

con.words: Ehrman invokes Christian belief in freely inhabited heaven without suffering to challenge any universal logical dependence between freedom and suffering.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman offers an internal Christian counterexample with sharply defined modal force: freedom and an absence of suffering are reportedly co-instantiated in heaven, challenging a universal necessity claim. Principal limitation: The argument does not establish that Swinburne accepts heavenly freedom as developmentally independent of earthly formation, leaving open the later distinction between formative choice and settled good character. Live burden: The counterexample tests the bare claim that freedom requires suffering; Swinburne bears the burden of showing why prior earthly formation is necessary, and Ehrman’s lack of a turn after that closing answer incurs no penalty. Locked score: 86/100 rewards the clear, responsive, and powerful counterexample, tempered because its ultimate force depends on the relevant conception of heavenly freedom and the merits of Swinburne’s temporally ordered reply.

pro.words: Swinburne distinguishes pastoral response from detached assessment, arguing that removing a disaster also removes moral opportunities within a world ordered toward sanctity.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Swinburne responsibly separates what should be said to bereaved people from philosophical assessment and insists that a counterfactual must include lost consequences rather than deleting disaster in isolation. Principal limitation: His appeal to sanctity supplies a value hierarchy but no comparative evidence that tsunami-scale destruction is necessary, proportionate, or beneficial for everyone involved, as his broad wording suggests. Live burden: He must justify the magnitude and distribution of harm, particularly for victims, without assuming that any generated opportunity outweighs every destroyed life, relationship, and possibility. Locked score: 71/100 acknowledges the relevant whole-world comparison and pastoral qualification, while reflecting weak warrant, overextension to all participants, and failure to complete the victim-benefit bridge for nonconsenting people whose ordinary goods and relationships are permanently lost.

con.words: Ehrman argues starving children lack the proposed cheerful choice and that observers’ character growth does not adequately justify victims’ deaths.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman separates benefits to observers from benefits to victims and identifies children unable to exercise the cheerful, character-forming choice invoked by Swinburne, exposing a specific justificatory gap. Principal limitation: The objection defeats the two stated rationales more directly than every possible subject-centered good, so it should not be expanded into proof that no additional justification could exist. Live burden: His side must keep the focus on who receives the alleged benefit while assessing Swinburne’s later usefulness claim and qualifications rather than assuming all character formation is irrelevant. Locked score: 87/100 rewards decisive victim-centered responsiveness, conceptual clarity, and proportionate scope, with limited evidentiary reserve because the numerical prevalence claim remains unverified debate testimony rather than established statistical evidence about the affected population.

pro.words: Swinburne claims involuntary usefulness may benefit sufferers, while denying it is necessarily overwhelming, greatest, or sufficient as his sole justification.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Swinburne relocates at least one alleged good within the sufferer’s own life and carefully preserves three important limits: usefulness is not necessarily overwhelming, greatest, or his complete justification. Principal limitation: The soldier comparison derives intuitive support from culturally honored, often voluntary service and does not establish that unknowing, nonconsenting victims receive an overall benefit sufficient to authorize extreme harm. Live burden: He must defend why usefulness belongs to the victim rather than merely to beneficiaries, compare it with the victim’s losses, and supply the additional reasons his qualification openly requires. Locked score: 73/100 credits precision, responsiveness, and commendable restraint, while reflecting weak analogical warrant and the continuing gap between partial value and the earlier overall-benefit condition.

con.words: Ehrman stresses Holocaust victims’ nonconsent, concedes human perpetrators caused their suffering, and denies that others’ nobility establishes benefit or justification for victims.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman combines nonconsent, forced suffering, and the distinction between perpetrators’ agency and victims’ welfare into the debate’s strongest concrete test of Swinburne’s usefulness and permission account. Principal limitation: The example powerfully challenges the presented justification, but Ehrman only briefly articulates the broader principle governing when an involuntary contribution could qualify as subject-centered benefit. Live burden: He must preserve the concession that humans caused the atrocity while showing why God’s permission remains unjustified under Swinburne’s own benefit condition, without confusing a defense of divine permission with the separate assertion that God directly killed the victims. Locked score: 88/100 reflects exceptional relevance, responsiveness, and moral clarity, with minor reserve because the general principle behind the compelling case remains comparatively undeveloped.

pro.words: Swinburne answers nonconsent with a hypothesized preference for useful suffering, distinguishes divine permission from killing, and defends historically consequential choices through a whole-world counterfactual.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Swinburne addresses several live objections rather than evading them, distinguishing permission from direct causation and explaining how vulnerability gives centuries of human choices serious historical significance. Principal limitation: His crucial supposition about what not-yet-created victims would prefer is speculative, and the loss of consequential choice does not establish that victims receive the overall benefit his own moral condition demands. Live burden: He must justify the hypothesized preference, compare the no-atrocity world fairly, and show why meaningful responsibility requires harms of this extremity instead of constrained alternatives. Locked score: 68/100 recognizes broad responsiveness and an identifiable counterfactual structure, but heavily discounts unsupported consent substitution, weak victim-centered warrant, and compressed reasoning within the overlapping exchange.

pro.words: Swinburne accepts biblical diversity but assigns different explanations to different evils, adding character formation in Hebrews and disclosed goodness in John.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Swinburne concedes the textual plurality, offers a coherent complementary-purpose interpretation, and supplies specific Hebrews and John examples instead of denying the diversity Ehrman documents. Principal limitation: Different explanations can coexist, but allocating them to different evils does not resolve cases where authors appear to assign opposed causal responsibility to suffering, and the textual interpretations remain compressed. Live burden: He must demonstrate that the accounts concern compatible levels, events, or purposes rather than merely asserting multiple good reasons under a later church synthesis. Locked score: 81/100 rewards direct engagement, concrete scriptural examples, and charitable acceptance of plurality, moderated because compatibility is clearer than authorial agreement or independent support for the proposed harmonization.

con.words: Ehrman surveys punishment, wrongdoing, redemption, hostile powers, mystery, and Ecclesiastes, arguing scripture offers diverse rather than straightforwardly unified explanations.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman presents a wide, differentiated taxonomy of biblical responses, identifies their contrasting causes and purposes, and carefully reserves the stronger inconsistency claim for a more specific later comparison. Principal limitation: The survey compresses textual detail and representativeness, while diversity alone does not show that several explanations cannot be complementary or apply to different kinds of suffering. Live burden: He must identify genuine conflicts rather than rely on plurality, distinguish his personal affinity with Ecclesiastes from proof, and answer Swinburne’s different-evils interpretation. Locked score: 85/100 reflects strong evidence within the debate, clear organization, high relevance, and good calibration, with a reservation for abbreviated exegesis and the limited inference available from taxonomy by itself without closer analysis of the authors’ historical settings and intended claims.

pro.words: Swinburne distinguishes proximate hostile agency from ultimate divine permission, arguing prophetic and apocalyptic causal descriptions therefore need not contradict one another.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Swinburne identifies a genuine logical distinction between immediate hostile causation and ultimate divine permission, directly answering Ehrman’s claim that the two scriptural frameworks are incompatible. Principal limitation: Possible reconciliation through causal levels does not establish that the relevant biblical authors intended that reconciliation, and the asserted predominance of a church interpretation receives little textual support here. Live burden: He must defend the interpretive bridge rather than merely show logical consistency, while keeping church synthesis distinct from Ehrman’s historical question about authorial expectations. Locked score: 79/100 rewards concise logical responsiveness and conceptual clarity, while discounting thin evidentiary warrant, overconfident interpretive prevalence, and the remaining distance between compatibility and adequate scriptural explanation.

con.words: Ehrman argues that prophetic attribution of suffering to God conflicts with apocalyptic attribution to hostile powers, challenging Swinburne’s complementary-diversity account.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman converts general biblical diversity into a precise causal conflict, contrasting prophetic attribution of suffering to God with apocalyptic attribution to hostile powers opposed to God. Principal limitation: The argument establishes a prima facie authorial tension but does not show that the relevant texts exclude layered causation, particularly Swinburne’s distinction between proximate hostile agency and ultimate divine permission. Live burden: He must support the claimed historical-authorial incompatibility rather than assume that opposed immediate agents exhaust the theological account, while keeping later church harmonization distinct from the original authors’ purposes, audiences, and conceptual worlds. Locked score: 85/100 rewards the narrow, responsive, and clearly articulated challenge, with moderated warrant because textual detail is compressed and the proposed permission reconciliation remains logically available without thereby being historically demonstrated.

pro.words: Swinburne separates incarnation as sharing permitted danger from redemption as reparation through Christ’s well-lived life and consequent death, without promising immediate relief.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Swinburne gives a distinctly Christian account with careful internal distinctions: God shares exposed suffering through incarnation, while Christ’s life and consequent death provide reparation rather than an immediate termination of suffering. Principal limitation: The war and vandalism analogies illustrate solidarity and payment but do not independently justify divine permission, representative reparation, or the connection between redemption from sin and observed suffering. Live burden: He must defend those theological premises and explain how delayed redemption contributes to adequate explanation rather than merely restating doctrine, while preserving his explicit no-immediate-end qualification. Locked score: 79/100 credits substantial development, precision, and calibrated scope, moderated by analogical compression and an incomplete bridge from solidarity and reparation to present suffering.

con.words: Ehrman contrasts incarnation’s claimed solidarity and salvation with continued disaster, disease, genocide, and apparently ineffective prayer, asking for evidence of present divine intervention.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman distinguishes shared suffering from effective intervention and presses a relevant evidential question about what observable difference incarnation and salvation make amid continuing disaster, disease, and genocide. Principal limitation: Continued suffering does not establish that no intervention occurs, and his broad statement that prayer does not matter outruns the comparative evidence offered in the exchange. Live burden: He must frame persistence as counterevidence rather than categorical disproof, while engaging Swinburne’s claim that redemption has delayed and nonpreventive purposes. Locked score: 80/100 recognizes a clear, motion-relevant challenge and concrete examples, but discounts causal overreach, limited evidence about prayer, and the gap between apparent nonintervention and a demonstrated absence of divine action across the very different cases that he groups together.

pro.words: Swinburne locates kingdom fulfillment in Christ’s resurrection and accepted sacrifice, concedes early imminence expectations, and invokes parables permitting delayed final completion.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Swinburne answers both fulfillment and timing, treats resurrection as a real and major change, and candidly acknowledges that many early Christians expected the end of suffering soon. Principal limitation: Invoking unspecified delay parables and fulfillment through resurrection does not fully reconcile the quoted imminent expectation or explain the continued suffering emphasized by Ehrman. Live burden: He must connect those parables to the disputed saying, clarify the scope of coming in power, and show why delayed completion remains an adequate rather than indefinitely flexible explanation. Locked score: 77/100 credits responsiveness, theological coherence, and an important historical concession, while reflecting limited textual warrant and the unresolved distance between resurrection, expected timing, and observable relief from the kinds of suffering that motivated the original challenge.

con.words: Ehrman distinguishes Swinburne’s church synthesis from biblical authors’ expectations and argues that an imminent suffering-ending kingdom did not arrive as anticipated.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman keeps authorial interpretation distinct from later church theology, cites a concrete imminent-kingdom saying, and connects continued suffering to the claimed nonfulfillment of early expectations. Principal limitation: His appeal to professional judgment and broad statements about biblical authors compress the textual comparison, while the conclusion depends on how coming in power and fulfillment are interpreted. Live burden: He must support the historical expectation without treating his expertise as sufficient and address Swinburne’s resurrection and delay-parable response on its actual terms. Locked score: 84/100 rewards strong relevance, specificity, and direct engagement with both textual basis and historical outcome, tempered by abbreviated exegesis and unresolved interpretive alternatives concerning reference, audience, chronology, and the proposed stages of fulfillment.

sections.title: Practical response, heaven, and final choice

pro.words: Swinburne argues earthly consequential freedom forms character suited for heaven, where settled goodness can later coexist with no serious possibility of evil.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Swinburne directly answers the heaven counterexample by distinguishing two temporally ordered goods, formative earthly choice and subsequently settled good character, rather than denying heavenly freedom. Principal limitation: The sequence relies on theological assumptions about entry and character formation and does not show that severe earthly suffering is necessary or proportionate to producing the relevant fitness. Live burden: His side must connect actual harms to this developmental mechanism and defend why less destructive formation would be inadequate, while no penalty can attach to Ehrman’s lack of a later reply opportunity. Locked score: 84/100 reflects a coherent, precise, highly responsive closing answer, moderated by limited independent warrant and the continuing proportionality problem for children, disaster victims, and others who seemingly receive no formative opportunity.

con.words: Ehrman separates explanatory uncertainty from practical agency, urging concrete action against homelessness, disease, poverty, and starvation rather than passive speculation.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman clearly distinguishes lacking a perfectly satisfying explanation from the capacity and obligation to respond, grounding his conclusion in concrete forms of relief rather than resignation or passivity. Principal limitation: Practical action completes a subsidiary burden but does not itself prove that Christian explanations are inadequate, and Job and Ecclesiastes receive only brief support for the stronger epistemic conclusion. Live burden: His side must keep humanitarian response separate from the motion-level explanatory verdict while preserving the corrected claim that people can respond and avoiding any invented contradiction. Locked score: 83/100 rewards clarity, calibration, and constructive practical relevance, tempered because the action recommendation bears indirectly on the central adequacy dispute and cannot independently settle which account of evil is intellectually satisfying.

pro.words: Swinburne’s parable contrasts passive intense pleasure with painful participation in great good, arguing experiential comfort is not the sole measure of life’s value.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Swinburne offers a vivid subject-centered comparison showing why comfort and pleasant experience need not exhaust the value of a life, and the conclusion follows within the constructed choice. Principal limitation: Voluntary childbirth-like valuable pain does not generalize straightforwardly to involuntary victims, while the selective alternatives and his word surely overstate agreement about the contested comparison. Live burden: He must explain how the parable bears on nonconsenting sufferers, demonstrate comparable goods in actual cases, and avoid letting hypothetical preference replace the earlier overall-benefit requirement. Locked score: 72/100 credits intelligibility, relevance, and memorable illustration, while discounting weak analogy, constrained alternatives, and failure to resolve the debate’s strongest victim-centered objections about consent, proportionality, compensation, and the distribution of supposed benefits.

strengths: Distinguished logical compatibility from physical limitation and built a cumulative account around consequential responsibility, character formation, sanctity, and subject-centered value.
Preserved significant qualifications: victim benefit conditions divine permission, usefulness is neither necessarily overwhelming nor his sole reason, and redemption promises no immediate relief.
Answered the heaven objection with a temporally ordered account of formative earthly freedom followed by settled heavenly character, while endorsing practical relief.

blunders.text: Relied on speculative victim preference and underdefended analogies to move from valuable responsibility to permission of nonconsenting victims’ extreme suffering.
Repeatedly identified possible goods without demonstrating their necessity, proportionality, or sufficient benefit for victims in famine, disaster, and atrocity.

strengths: Tested Swinburne’s own benefit condition against natural evil and nonconsenting victims while conceding the genuine relevance of free will to human-caused suffering.
Used heaven as an internal counterexample and sharpened biblical diversity into a specific conflict over causal responsibility and unfulfilled imminent expectations.
Closed constructively by distinguishing explanatory uncertainty from people’s continuing ability and obligation to reduce concrete suffering.

blunders.text: Sometimes moved too quickly from persistent suffering to broad claims that prayer does not matter or that intervention is absent, without comparative evidence.
Compressed several historical and authorial claims into professional judgment, leaving the textual basis less developed than the philosophical victim-centered objections.

finalArgument.thesis: Christian doctrines can jointly explain a temporally bounded world of consequential freedom when divine solidarity, victim-centered value, and reparative restoration govern what permission ultimately means.
premises: Responsibility has distinctive value when choices genuinely affect others, because harmless simulation cannot create the same accountability, dependence, or historically consequential moral authorship.
Permission of suffering is morally defensible only where each victim retains significant subject-centered goods, eventual restoration, and a life whose value is not exhausted by immediate experience.
Natural regularity and vulnerability make coherent action possible, while predictable divine cancellation of every grave consequence would erode both responsibility and practical concern for others.

Incarnation adds moral solidarity because a creator who permits costly conditions shares them, while redemption offers reparation and restored relationship rather than an immediate preventive mechanism.
Heaven can complete rather than contradict the process if freely formed character persists into a condition where goodness is stable and losses are genuinely repaired.
finalArgument.conclusion: On those conditions, the Christian account forms a positive cumulative explanation: stable creaturely agency creates real responsibility, incarnation shares its costs, and heaven can preserve character while repairing each victim’s losses.

newArguments.title: Relational agency structure
newArguments.text: Consequential freedom creates more than isolated choices: it makes creatures answerable to one another within a stable order where protection, rescue, dependence, and trust are possible. Constant divine cancellation of harmful outcomes would alter that shared moral structure by transferring final responsibility from creatures to predictable intervention. This gives the Christian account an affirmative reason for some divine restraint while leaving a strict boundary: the inference does not show that actual atrocities are proportionate, and extreme losses still require victim-specific restoration rather than appeal to other people’s growth.

newArguments.title: Victim continuity and repair
newArguments.text: Benefits accruing to observers cannot by themselves authorize a victim’s suffering, but a creator could owe each sufferer continuing agency, memory, relationship, and opportunities to appropriate or reject the meaning of what occurred. Restoration would then differ from compensation by preserving the victim as an active participant rather than replacing a lost life with unrelated pleasure. This inference strengthens Swinburne’s creator-right claim only if post-suffering existence is personal, reparative, and responsive to the particular deprivation; generic afterlife benefit would not establish permission.

finalArgument.thesis: Christian explanations remain inadequate when possible goods fail to show why victims bear these harms, why lesser harms would not suffice, or why expected intervention remains hidden.
premises: Logical compatibility shows only that divine attributes and suffering might coexist, whereas adequacy requires comparative reasons for the actual scale, distribution, and apparent randomness of suffering.
Goods produced through responsibility or character cannot justify victims unless those victims receive sufficient benefit and are not subordinated to observers’ development or perpetrators’ choices.
Heaven places pressure on necessity claims because Christianity already envisions valuable agency without continuing suffering, even if a developmental sequence offers a possible reply.
Scriptural plurality becomes evidentially costly when authorial frameworks assign suffering to opposed agents or expect imminent relief that later theology must reinterpret.
Practical relief remains rational without a final explanation, demonstrating that moral response need not wait for confidence in providential purpose.
finalArgument.conclusion: The proportionate conclusion is not deductive atheism but withheld acceptance: the offered Christian account leaves victim benefit, proportionality, textual conflict, and apparent nonintervention materially unresolved.

newArguments.title: Least-harm counterfactual
newArguments.text: Every claimed good should be tested against the nearest world that preserves it with less suffering. If courage requires danger, responsibility requires consequences, or compassion requires need, the question is whether those goods require starvation, tsunami, genocide, and childhood death at their actual intensity. The critic need not design a perfect world; identifying a nearby alternative with comparable agency and materially reduced irreversible harm shifts the burden back to the explanation. An adequate theodicy must show why the lesser-harm alternative loses a good sufficient to justify the difference.

newArguments.title: Explanatory elasticity cost
newArguments.text: An explanation loses force when opposite observations fit it equally well. Immediate relief can be called intervention, continued suffering can be called character formation, early fulfillment can be located in resurrection, and indefinite delay can be absorbed by parables. Each move may be individually coherent, yet together they risk making the account insensitive to evidence. Christianity would answer this objection by stating in advance what patterns of suffering, intervention, restoration, or historical fulfillment its explanation makes more likely and what conceivable pattern would count against it.

noveltyMap.title: Relational agency structure
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Derives a shared moral structure of protection, rescue, dependence, and trust from stable consequential agency, while retaining victim-specific limits on divine restraint.

noveltyMap.title: Victim continuity and repair
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Derives a victim-specific restoration requirement involving continuing agency and particularized repair rather than observer benefit or generic compensation.

noveltyMap.title: Least-harm counterfactual
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Introduces a nearest-world comparison requiring each alleged good to justify the marginal suffering beyond a less harmful agency-preserving alternative.

noveltyMap.title: Explanatory elasticity cost
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Adds an evidential sensitivity test asking which observations the Christian explanation predicts and what outcomes would count against it.
